content: Urticaria, commonly referred to as hives, is a prevalent skin condition characterized by the presence of itchy, raised welts that can appear on various parts of the body. There are multiple subtypes of urticaria, and a variety of treatment options are available. However, there is no consensus regarding the effectiveness of histamine H2-receptor antagonists in managing this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of H2-receptor antagonists in the treatment of urticaria. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of several databases was conducted up to October 7, 2011. These databases included the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL in The Cochrane Library (2011, Issue 4), MEDLINE (from 2005), EMBASE (from 2007), and LILACS (from 1982). Additionally, online trial registries were searched for ongoing studies. The review included randomized controlled trials that investigated the use of H2-receptor antagonists in individuals with a clinical diagnosis of urticaria, regardless of the duration or subtype of the condition. Studies that focused on H1-antihistamines for chronic urticaria were excluded, as they are the subject of a separate Cochrane review. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data for analysis. Ultimately, four studies involving a total of 144 participants were included in the review. These studies were relatively small in size and were categorized as having a high to unclear risk of bias. The findings indicated that a combination of ranitidine and diphenhydramine was more effective in resolving urticaria compared to diphenhydramine alone, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.59 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.07 to 2.36. While there was some improvement in symptoms such as itching, weal size, and intensity, cimetidine did not demonstrate a statistically significant overall improvement in urticaria symptoms when compared to diphenhydramine. However, a combination of cimetidine and diphenhydramine was found to be more effective than diphenhydramine alone, with an RR of 2.02 and a 95% CI of 1.03 to 3.94. Adverse events were reported with several of the interventions. Both ranitidine and diphenhydramine were associated with drowsiness and sedation. However, there was no significant difference in the level of sedation from baseline when comparing famotidine to diphenhydramine. The authors concluded that the evidence provided by this review is very limited, as it is based on a small number of older studies with significant methodological limitations. The high to unclear risk of bias in these studies further weakens the reliability of the findings. As a result, the review does not provide sufficient evidence to make confident decisions regarding the use of H2-receptor antagonists for the treatment of urticaria. While some studies reported mild symptom relief and minimal clinical improvement in certain participants, the overall evidence is weak and imprecise. The authors emphasized the limitations and lack of precision in the available data throughout the review.
